findings.heading: Plot with `ggplotly()`
findings.proposition: English says the reader toggles series by clicking the different items in the LEGEND; the Turkish says to click the different items in the PLOT ("Grafikteki farkli ogelere tiklamayi deneyin").
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader clicks the stacked bars in the plot area, where nothing appears or disappears, and concludes the interactive legend toggling described in the text does not work.

findings.heading: Heat tiles
findings.proposition: English says the plot displays the PROPORTION of days per week that facilities reported data; the Turkish says the plot visualises "the data obtained from facilities on some days of the week" ("haftanin bazi gunlerinde tesislerden elde edilen veriler"), which is a different quantity and is contradicted by the chunk beside it (p_days_reported, title "Percent of days per week that facility reported data").
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader misreads the heat tile fill scale as counts or values collected on selected weekdays, rather than as a reporting-completeness percentage, and therefore misinterprets every tile in the figure.

findings.heading: Heat tiles
findings.proposition: English says the facilities report data TO THEIR PROVINCE; the Turkish instead states the facilities are ESTABLISHED IN certain provinces ("belirli illerde kurulmus olan malarya tesisleri").
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader loses the reporting relationship that the figure is about, and reads the province only as a location filter rather than as the recipient of the reports being counted.

findings.heading: Plot with `ggplotly()`
findings.proposition: English states the last toolbar control adjusts whether data show WHEN YOU ARE NOT HOVERING ON THE LINE; the Turkish drops that condition and says only "adjust settings about whether data are shown".
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader does not learn which hover state the button governs, so cannot tell what changes when the button is pressed and may confuse it with the spike-line toggle listed above it.

findings.heading: Resources
findings.proposition: English says plotly works with really ANY data science language BECAUSE it is built in JavaScript; the Turkish says it works with "any JavaScript-based data science coding language", turning the reason into a restriction on which languages qualify.
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader concludes plotly is limited to JavaScript-based languages and may not look for the Python, Julia or MATLAB bindings that the English sentence points them toward.

findings.heading: Start with a `ggplot()`
findings.proposition: English calls `linelist` the case line list DATASET used in many pages of the handbook; the Turkish calls it the `linelist` METHOD ("`linelist` metodunu kullanarak").
findings.reader_consequence: A Turkish reader may look for a function or method named linelist instead of recognising the imported data frame that the next section loads with appliedepidata::get_data().

findings.heading: Plot with `ggplotly()`
findings.proposition: The Turkish adds that the summary dataset contains the NUMBER of cases with a known outcome ("ciktilari bilinen vakalarin sayisi") as a listed element; the English names only the epidemiological week and the percent of known-outcome cases that died.
findings.reader_consequence: None harmful: the added element matches the n_known_outcome column in the chunk below, but the Turkish inventory of the summary dataset no longer matches the English one.
